claim: S1PR1 activation by S1P promotes lymphocyte egress from lymphoid organs.
source: The activation of Sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor 1 (S1PR1) by S1P promotes lymphocyte egress from lymphoid organs, a process critical for immune surveillance and T cell effector activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about S1PR1 function.

claim: Multiple drugs that inhibit S1PR1 function are in clinical use for treating autoimmune diseases.
source: Multiple drugs that inhibit S1PR1 function are in use clinically for the treatment of autoimmune diseases.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: CD69 is an endogenous negative regulator of lymphocyte egress.
source: Cluster of Differentiation 69 (CD69) is an endogenous negative regulator of lymphocyte egress that interacts with S1PR1 in cis to facilitate internalization and degradation of the receptor.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior literature.

claim: CD69 interacts with S1PR1 in cis to facilitate internalization and degradation of the receptor.
source: Cluster of Differentiation 69 (CD69) is an endogenous negative regulator of lymphocyte egress that interacts with S1PR1 in cis to facilitate internalization and degradation of the receptor.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior literature.

claim: The mechanism by which CD69 causes S1PR1 internalization has been unclear.
source: The mechanism by which CD69 causes S1PR1 internalization has been unclear.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a knowledge gap.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of CD69-bound S1PR1 coupled to heterotrimeric Gi complex was determined at 3.15 Å resolution.
source: Here, we present the cryo-EM structure of CD69-bound S1PR1 coupled to the heterotrimeric Gi complex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the structural data presented in the results.

claim: The transmembrane helix of one protomer of CD69 homodimer contacts S1PR1-TM4.
source: The transmembrane helix (TM) of one protomer of CD69 homodimer contacts the S1PR1-TM4.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 1C and Figure 2A-B.

claim: CD69 binding allosterically induces the movement of S1PR1-TMs 5-6.
source: This interaction allosterically induces the movement of S1PR1-TMs 5–6, directly activating the receptor to engage the heterotrimeric Gi.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 3.

claim: CD69 directly activates S1PR1 to engage heterotrimeric Gi.
source: This interaction allosterically induces the movement of S1PR1-TMs 5–6, directly activating the receptor to engage the heterotrimeric Gi.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by GTPase assay data in Figure 1A.

claim: Mutations in key residues at the CD69-S1PR1 interface affect the interactions between CD69 and S1PR1.
source: Mutations in key residues at the interface affect the interactions between CD69 and S1PR1, as well as reduce the receptor internalization.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: Mutations in key residues at the CD69-S1PR1 interface reduce receptor internalization.
source: Mutations in key residues at the interface affect the interactions between CD69 and S1PR1, as well as reduce the receptor internalization.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: CD69 acts in cis as a protein agonist of S1PR1.
source: Thus, our structural findings along with functional analyses demonstrate that CD69 acts in cis as a protein agonist of S1PR1, thereby promoting Gi-dependent S1PR1 internalization, loss of S1P gradient sensing, and inhibition of lymphocyte egress.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by structural and functional data throughout the manuscript.

claim: CD69 promotes Gi-dependent S1PR1 internalization.
source: Thus, our structural findings along with functional analyses demonstrate that CD69 acts in cis as a protein agonist of S1PR1, thereby promoting Gi-dependent S1PR1 internalization, loss of S1P gradient sensing, and inhibition of lymphocyte egress.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4E-F showing PTX reduces CD69-mediated internalization.

claim: CD69 causes loss of S1P gradient sensing.
source: Thus, our structural findings along with functional analyses demonstrate that CD69 acts in cis as a protein agonist of S1PR1, thereby promoting Gi-dependent S1PR1 internalization, loss of S1P gradient sensing, and inhibition of lymphocyte egress.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a consequence of CD69 action.

claim: CD69 inhibits lymphocyte egress.
source: Thus, our structural findings along with functional analyses demonstrate that CD69 acts in cis as a protein agonist of S1PR1, thereby promoting Gi-dependent S1PR1 internalization, loss of S1P gradient sensing, and inhibition of lymphocyte egress.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior literature cited in the introduction.

claim: S1P plays an essential role in promoting lymphocyte egress from lymphoid organs into blood and lymph via interaction with S1PR1.
source: Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) plays an essential role in the immune system by promoting the egress of lymphocytes from lymphoid organs into blood and lymph via a direct interaction with one of its five cognate G protein–coupled receptors, S1PR1 (Baeyens and Schwab, 2020; Cartier and Hla, 2019; Cyster and Schwab, 2012; Pappu et al., 2007; Rosen et al., 2013; Spiegel and Milstien, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: After egressing from lymphoid tissues, T and B lymphocytes travel to other lymphoid organs in a cycle of continual pathogen surveillance.
source: After egressing from spleen, lymph nodes, or mucosal lymphoid tissues, T and B lymphocytes travel to other lymphoid organs in a cycle of continual pathogen surveillance.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: During infection, there is a temporary shutdown of lymphocyte egress from responding lymphoid organs.
source: When an infection occurs, there is a temporary shutdown of lymphocyte egress from the responding lymphoid organ(s) and this enables increased accumulation of lymphocytes and enhances the immune response (Cyster and Schwab, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Egress shutdown enables increased accumulation of lymphocytes and enhances the immune response.
source: When an infection occurs, there is a temporary shutdown of lymphocyte egress from the responding lymphoid organ(s) and this enables increased accumulation of lymphocytes and enhances the immune response (Cyster and Schwab, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Egress shutdown is mediated by type I interferon inducing lymphocyte CD69 expression.
source: Egress shutdown is mediated by type I interferon (IFN) inducing lymphocyte CD69 expression.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: CD69 is a type II transmembrane C-type lectin protein.
source: CD69, a type II transmembrane C-type lectin protein, intrinsically inhibits the function of S1PR1 in T and B cells (Shiow et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: CD69 intrinsically inhibits the function of S1PR1 in T and B cells.
source: CD69, a type II transmembrane C-type lectin protein, intrinsically inhibits the function of S1PR1 in T and B cells (Shiow et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: CD69 regulates T cell egress from the thymus.
source: CD69 also regulates T cell egress from the thymus (Nakayama et al., 2002; Zachariah and Cyster, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A disulfide bond in the extracellular domain links CD69 as a homodimer.
source: A disulfide-bond in the extracellular domain links CD69 as a homodimer (Ziegler et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: CD69 may associate with S1PR1 through interactions between their transmembrane domains.
source: Biochemical studies demonstrated that CD69 may associate with S1PR1 through interactions between their transmembrane domains (TMs) to facilitate S1PR1 internalization and degradation (Bankovich et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: CD69 binds S1PR1 but not the other S1PRs.
source: Unlike S1P, CD69 has been shown to bind S1PR1 but not the other S1PRs (Bankovich et al., 2010; Jenne et al., 2009; Shiow et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Several S1PR1 modulators (Fingolimod, Siponimod, Ozanimod, and Etrasimod) have been approved for treating multiple sclerosis and ulcerative colitis.
source: Importantly, several S1PR1 modulators (e.g. Fingolimod, also known as FTY720, Siponimod, Ozanimod, and Etrasimod), have been approved for treating the autoimmune diseases multiple sclerosis and ulcerative colitis (Brinkmann et al., 2010; Chun et al., 2021; Dal Buono et al., 2022; Kappos et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: S1PR1 immunosuppressants act by inhibiting S1PR1 function and preventing autoimmune effector lymphocytes from exiting lymphoid organs.
source: These immunosuppressants are believed to act by inhibiting S1PR1 function and thereby preventing autoimmune effector lymphocytes exiting lymphoid organs, blocking the autoimmune attack.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as the mechanism of action.

claim: Sphingosine or FTY720 is metabolically catalyzed by intracellular sphingosine kinases into the phosphorylated form.
source: Either sphingosine or FTY720 is metabolically catalyzed by two intracellular sphingosine kinases into the phosphorylated form (S1P or FTY720-P) and then exported to the extracellular space via S1P transporters (Baeyens and Schwab, 2020; Spiegel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: FTY720-P activates S1PR1 but causes persistent internalization and degradation of S1PR1.
source: There, S1P binds to its receptors for initiation of the signal while FTY720-P activates the S1PR1 but causes a persistent internalization and degradation of S1PR1 to attenuate the signal (Brinkmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of S1PR1 complexed with different small molecule ligands have been determined.
source: Recently, cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of S1PR1 complexed with different small molecule ligands have been determined (Liu et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The crystal structure of antagonist ML056-bound S1PR1 reveals its inactive state.
source: The previously determined crystal structure of antagonist ML056-bound S1PR1 reveals its inactive state (Hanson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Addition of CD69 alone caused a similar amount of Gi activation as addition of S1P.
source: Remarkably, addition of CD69 alone caused a similar amount of Gi activation as addition of S1P indicating that CD69 functions as a protein agonist of S1PR1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CD69 functions as a protein agonist of S1PR1.
source: Remarkably, addition of CD69 alone caused a similar amount of Gi activation as addition of S1P indicating that CD69 functions as a protein agonist of S1PR1 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by GTPase assay data in Figure 1A.

claim: The overall structure of the CD69-bound S1PR1 coupled to heterotrimeric Gi was determined at 3.15 Å resolution.
source: The overall structure of the CD69-bound S1PR1 coupled to heterotrimeric Gi was determined at 3.15 Å resolution by 293,516 particles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–F; Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Table 1.

claim: The structure shows that one S1PR1 binds one CD69 homodimer and one Gi heterotrimer.
source: The structure shows that one S1PR1 binds one CD69 homodimer and one Gi heterotrimer.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: The intracellular loop 3 (ICL3) and the C-terminus of S1PR1 and the intracellular and extracellular domains of CD69 were not found in the cryo-EM map.
source: The intracellular loop 3 (ICL3) and the C-terminus of S1PR1 and the intracellular and extracellular domains of CD69 were not found in the cryo-EM map indicating their flexibility in the complex.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation from the cryo-EM map.

claim: The TMs of the CD69 homodimer were clearly defined in the map owing to their interactions with S1PR1.
source: In contrast, the TMs of the CD69 homodimer were clearly defined in the map owing to their interactions with S1PR1 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; the interacting TM helix is referred to as CD69-a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There is no notable lipid ligand in the 7-TM bundle of S1PR1 in the CD69-bound structure.
source: Because no lipid was supplemented into the protein during the expression and purification, there is no notable lipid ligand in the 7-TM bundle of S1PR1, which is different from the previous structural discoveries on S1PRs (Chen et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation from the structure.

claim: The entire CD69-S1PR1-Gi complex and the S1P bound S1PR1-Gi complex share a similar conformation with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 0.82 Å.
source: Structural comparison shows that the entire complex and the S1P bound S1PR1-Gi complex share a similar conformation with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 0.82 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: F1614.43 in TM4 presents a notable shift due to CD69 binding.
source: The receptors in both complexes can be aligned well; however, the F1614.43 in TM4 presents a notable shift due to CD69 binding (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The modeled S1PR1 bound to the other TM of the CD69 homodimer would sterically clash with the Giα subunit.
source: We docked the S1PR1 bound to the other TM of the CD69 homodimer which showed that the modeled receptor would sterically clash with the Giα subunit (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Only one receptor binds one CD69 homodimer in the presence of the heterotrimeric G-protein due to steric clash.
source: This may explain why only one receptor binds one CD69 homodimer in the presence of the heterotrimeric G-protein.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the structural modeling.

claim: The TM of one protomer of CD69 homodimer interacts with the TM4 of S1PR1.
source: The TM of one protomer of CD69 homodimer interacts with the TM4 of S1PR1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The interface area between CD69 and S1PR1 TMs is about 600 Å2.
source: The interface area between TMs is about 600 Å2.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a measurement from the structure.

claim: Residues V41, V45, V48, V49, T52, I56, I59, A60 of CD69 mediate its extensive interactions with S1PR1.
source: Structural analysis shows that residues V41, V45, V48, V49, T52, I56, I59, A60 of CD69 mediate its extensive interactions with the receptor (Figure 2A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Residues L1604.42, F1614.43, I1644.46, W1684.50, V1694.51, L1724.54, I1734.55, G1764.58, I1794.61 and M1804.62 of S1PR1-TM4 contribute to the interaction with CD69.
source: Residues L1604.42, F1614.43, I1644.46, W1684.50, V1694.51, L1724.54, I1734.55, G1764.58, I1794.61 and M1804.62 of S1PR1-TM4 contribute to the interaction with CD69 (Figure 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The TM of another CD69 protomer does not have any interactions with the receptor and heterotrimeric Gi protein.
source: However, the TM of another CD69 does not have any interactions with the receptor and heterotrimeric Gi protein (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The heterotrimeric Gi proteins in CD69-bound and S1P-bound S1PR1 complexes exhibit a similar state with a RMSD of 0.45 Å.
source: Further structural comparison with the S1P-bound S1PR1-Gi complex indicates that the heterotrimeric Gi proteins in both complexes exhibit a similar state with a RMSD of 0.45 Å.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a structural comparison.

claim: S1P and CD69 stimulate the receptor to engage the heterotrimeric Gi proteins in an analogous fashion.
source: This finding implies that S1P and CD69 stimulate the receptor to engage the heterotrimeric Gi proteins in an analogous fashion.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the structural comparison.

claim: S1PR1 mutants V1694.51Y and M1804.62Y present reduced binding to CD69 compared to wild-type S1PR1.
source: Compared to the wild-type S1PR1, two mutants (V1694.51Y and M1804.62Y) present reduced binding to CD69 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: S1PR1 mutants V1694.51Y and M1804.62Y retained normal activity in response to S1P.
source: The TGFα shedding assay showed that these two mutants retained normal activity in response to S1P (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The interaction between S1PR1 and CD69 mutants V48F/V49F or I56F/I59F is considerably attenuated.
source: The co-IP results show that the interaction between S1PR1 and either mutant is considerably attenuated, thus directly supporting the role of CD69-TM in the complex assembly (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The activation of Gi proteins in the presence of CD69(V48F/V49F) or CD69(I56F/I59F) was decreased.
source: Consistent with the results of our co-IP assays, the activation of Gi proteins in the presence of either variant was decreased (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CD69(V48F/V49F) and CD69(I56F/I59F) were both reduced in their ability to downregulate S1PR1.
source: In accord with the biochemical data, CD69(V48F/V49F), and CD69(I56F/I59F) were both reduced in their ability to downregulate S1PR1 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The binding of CD69 induces a 4 Å shift at the intracellular end of TM4.
source: The binding of CD69 induces a 4 Å shift at the intracellular end of TM4 causing the residues C1674.49, I1704.52, and L1744.56 in TM4 to face TM3 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: C1674.49 and I1704.52 have hydrophobic contacts with F1333.41 in TM3.
source: C1674.49 and I1704.52 have hydrophobic contacts with the F1333.41 in TM3, and L1744.56 pushes the F2105.47 in TM5 towards the edge of the receptor to form the hydrophobic interactions with W2696.48 and F2736.52 in TM6 (Figure 3C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: L1744.56 pushes F2105.47 in TM5 towards the edge of the receptor to form hydrophobic interactions with W2696.48 and F2736.52 in TM6.
source: C1674.49 and I1704.52 have hydrophobic contacts with the F1333.41 in TM3, and L1744.56 pushes the F2105.47 in TM5 towards the edge of the receptor to form the hydrophobic interactions with W2696.48 and F2736.52 in TM6 (Figure 3C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: These interactions trigger the notable movement of TM5 and TM6 allowing the opening of intracellular regions to engage the heterotrimeric Gi proteins.
source: These interactions trigger the notable movement of TM5 and TM6 allowing the opening of intracellular regions to engage the heterotrimeric Gi proteins (Figure 3A and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A and D.

claim: Residues A1373.45, I1704.52, L1744.56, F2105.47, W2696.48, and F2736.52 are conserved among S1PR1, S1PR2 and S1PR3.
source: Residues A1373.45, I1704.52, L1744.56, F2105.47, W2696.48, and F2736.52 are conserved among S1PR1, S1PR2 and S1PR3, but not F1333.41 and C1674.49.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a sequence comparison observation.

claim: F1333.41 and C1674.49 are not conserved among S1PR1, S1PR2 and S1PR3.
source: Residues A1373.45, I1704.52, L1744.56, F2105.47, W2696.48, and F2736.52 are conserved among S1PR1, S1PR2 and S1PR3, but not F1333.41 and C1674.49.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a sequence comparison observation.

claim: Key residues crucial for S1P binding and receptor activation present similar conformations in S1P-bound S1PR1 and CD69-bound S1PR1 structures.
source: Remarkably, further comparison shows that the key residues, which are crucial for the S1P binding and receptor activation, present similar conformations in the structures of S1P-bound S1PR1 and CD69-bound S1PR1, although S1P and CD69 have different structural natures and completely distinct binding sites in the receptor (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CD69 specifically binds to S1PR1, and does not associate with S1PR2, S1PR3 or S1PR5.
source: Previous work showed that CD69 specifically binds to S1PR1, and it does not associate with S1PR2, S1PR3 or S1PR5 (Bankovich et al., 2010; Jenne et al., 2009; Shiow et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: There is a very weak interaction between S1PR2 and CD69.
source: To dissect the binding specificity of CD69, we carried out the co-IP assays to show a very weak interaction between S1PR2 and CD69 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Residues L1574.51 and L1684.62 in S1PR2-TM4 are determinants for specific recognition of CD69.
source: Although the sequence homology among five S1PRs is high, residues L1574.51 and L1684.62 in S1PR2-TM4 are not conserved with those in S1PR1 and are determinants for specific recognition of CD69 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: S1PR2(L1574.51V/L1684.62M) could interact with CD69 albeit the interactions are weaker than that between S1PR1 and CD69.
source: Our co-IP result clearly shows that S1PR2(L1574.51V/L1684.62M) could interact with CD69 albeit the interactions are weaker than that between S1PR1 and CD69 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The CD69 binding site is akin to that of allosteric agents which attach to receptors.
source: Interestingly, the CD69 binding site is akin to that of the allosteric agents which attach to receptors (Draper-Joyce et al., 2021; Mao et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2022), although the nature of these agents and CD69 is quite different.
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations.

claim: CD69 binds to the edge of S1PR1 and acts as a protein agonist to directly activate the receptor in the absence of any agonists in the orthosteric site.
source: CD69 binds to the edge of S1PR1, but it acts as a protein agonist to directly activate the receptor in the absence of any agonists in the orthosteric site.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: When Ex26 (an S1PR1 antagonist) was added to cells, only ~50% receptors were internalized compared to ~80% without Ex26.
source: After 24 hr, the fluorescence images show that substantial receptors (~80%) have been internalized with CD69. However, when we added the Ex26, a potent S1PR1 antagonist (Cahalan et al., 2013), into the cells 6 hr after transfection, the images show that just ~50% receptors have been internalized (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: CD69-mediated S1PR1 activation could be reversed when the 7-TMs pocket is preoccupied by an antagonist.
source: This finding indicates that the CD69-mediated S1PR1 activation could be reversed when the 7-TMs pocket is preoccupied by an antagonist.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from the Ex26 experiment.

claim: Barbadin does not interfere with CD69-induced receptor internalization.
source: The results show that Barbadin does not interfere with CD69-induced receptor internalization (Figure 4C and D), but PTX could prevent half of the receptors from internalization (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: PTX could prevent half of the receptors from internalization.
source: The results show that Barbadin does not interfere with CD69-induced receptor internalization (Figure 4C and D), but PTX could prevent half of the receptors from internalization (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: CD69 agonism of S1PR1 induces Gi-dependent internalization of the complex.
source: Thus, CD69 agonism of S1PR1 induces Gi-dependent internalization of the complex.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the PTX experiment.

claim: Barbadin was effective in reducing FTY70-P-induced S1PR1 internalization.
source: Our finding also supports that Barbadin was effective in reducing FTY70-P-induced S1PR1 internalization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CD69 is strongly transcriptionally induced in lymphocytes within an hour of exposure to type I IFN, TLR ligands, or antigen receptor engagement.
source: As an immediate early gene, CD69 is strongly transcriptionally induced in lymphocytes within an hour of exposure to type I IFN, toll-like receptor (TLR) ligands, or antigen receptor engagement (Grigorova et al., 2010; Shiow et al., 2006; Ziegler et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Following induction, CD69 protein engages S1PR1 as an agonist, causing S1PR1 internalization and loss of the ability to sense S1P gradients.
source: Following induction, CD69 protein engages S1PR1 as an agonist, causing S1PR1 internalization and loss of the ability to sense S1P gradients.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Even prior to internalization, CD69 disrupts S1PR1's egress promoting function by acting as a high concentration agonist.
source: We speculate that even prior to internalization, CD69 disrupts S1PR1's egress promoting function by acting as a high concentration agonist and thus making the receptor 'blind' to S1P distribution.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation.

claim: Correctly distributed S1P and correctly localized S1PR1 activation are critical for effective lymphocyte egress.
source: Consistently, our functional analysis reveals that CD69 could not synergize with S1P to trigger S1PR1 activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). Previous work has shown the critical importance of correctly distributed S1P and thus correctly localized S1PR1 activation for effective lymphocyte egress (Schwab et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: CD69 could not synergize with S1P to trigger S1PR1 activation.
source: Consistently, our functional analysis reveals that CD69 could not synergize with S1P to trigger S1PR1 activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: S1PR1 transmits signals needed for maintaining T cell survival.
source: As well as promoting egress, S1PR1, transmits signals needed for maintaining T cell survival (Mendoza et al., 2017) and CD69 has been implicated in transmitting signals that influence T cell differentiation (Cibrián and Sánchez-Madrid, 2017; Kimura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: CD69 has been implicated in transmitting signals that influence T cell differentiation.
source: As well as promoting egress, S1PR1, transmits signals needed for maintaining T cell survival (Mendoza et al., 2017) and CD69 has been implicated in transmitting signals that influence T cell differentiation (Cibrián and Sánchez-Madrid, 2017; Kimura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: GRK2 and dynamin participate in S1PR1 internalization in response to S1P.
source: GRK2 (Arnon et al., 2011; Oo et al., 2007; Watterson et al., 2002) and dynamin (Willinger et al., 2014) participate in S1PR1 internalization in response to S1P.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: GRK2 and dynamin may have a role in CD69-mediated S1PR1 internalization.
source: In accord with these factors possibly having a role in CD69-mediated S1PR1 internalization, they have been shown to promote internalization of some receptors independently of β-arrestins (Moo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation with a supporting citation.

claim: The selectivity of CD69 for S1PR1 is important for allowing activated CD69+ lymphocytes and natural killer cells to employ other S1PRs without interruption by CD69.
source: The selectivity of CD69 for S1PR1 is important for allowing activated CD69+ lymphocytes and natural killer cells to employ other S1PRs, such as S1PR2 and S1PR5, to carry out functions without interruption by CD69 (Jenne et al., 2009; Laidlaw et al., 2019; Moriyama et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The lack of conservation of key residues in TM4 of S1PR2, S1PR5 and other S1PRs provides an explanation for CD69 selectivity.
source: The lack of conservation of key residues that mediate the S1PR1-CD69 interaction in TM4 of S1PR2, S1PR5 and the other S1PRs provides an explanation for this selectivity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: This study provides the first example of GPCR activation by interaction in cis with a transmembrane ligand.
source: In summary, we provide the first example of GPCR activation by interaction in cis with a transmembrane ligand and thereby explain the mechanism of lymphocyte egress shutdown.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: The structure offers insights that may enable introduction of transcriptionally inducible GPCR switches into CAR-T cells and other engineered cell types.
source: The structure also offers insights that may enable introduction of transcriptionally inducible GPCR switches into CAR-T cells and other engineered cell types.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a potential application.

claim: Human S1PR1 and CD69 were expressed in HEK293 cells cultured in medium with lipid-deficient serum.
source: Since serum contains an abundance of lipids including S1P, we expressed human S1PR1 or CD69 in HEK293 cells cultured in a medium with lipid-deficient serum.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a methodological detail.

claim: The interface area between CD69 and S1PR1 transmembrane domains is approximately 600 Å2.
source: The interface area between TMs is about 600 Å2.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a measurement from the structure.

claim: RAMP1 binds CLR class B GPCR to form the CGRP receptor involved in migraine pathology.
source: Receptor activity-modifying protein 1 (RAMP1), a type I transmembrane domain protein, binds the calcitonin receptor-like receptor (CLR) class B GPCR to form the Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) receptor which is involved in the pathology of migraine (Russell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: The TM of RAMP1 interacts with TMs 3-5 of CLR.
source: The structure of Gs-protein coupled CGRP receptor uncovers that TM of RAMP1 interacts with TMs 3–5 of CLR and the extracellular domains of RAMP1 and CLR have extensive interactions (Liang et al., 2018; Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Both CLR and RAMP1 contribute to the engagement of their agonist CGRP.
source: Both CLR and RAMP1 contribute to the engagement of their agonist CGRP.
evidence: This is stated in the results as established knowledge.

claim: The extracellular domain of CD69 is completely invisible in the complex and may not interact with the extracellular loops of S1PR1.
source: The extracellular domain of CD69 is completely invisible in the complex and may not interact with the extracellular loops of S1PR1.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation from the structure.

claim: mGlu2 employs TM4 to maintain its inactive dimeric state or TM6 to assemble as a homodimer in the presence of its agonist.
source: The metabotropic glutamate receptor 2 (mGlu2), a Class-C GPCR, employs TM4 to maintain its inactive dimeric state or TM6 to assemble as a homodimer in the presence of its agonist (Du et al., 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: TM5 plays a key role in the assembly of inactive mGlu2-mGlu7 heterodimer.
source: The structure of inactive mGlu2–mGlu7 heterodimer shows that TM5 plays a key role in the complex assembly (Du et al., 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: TM1 of the class D GPCR Ste2 is responsible for engaging the TM1 of another Ste2 to form a homodimer.
source: Moreover, TM1 of the class D GPCR Ste2 is responsible for engaging the TM1 of another Ste2 to form a homodimer (Velazhahan et al., 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: GPCRs could employ distinct TMs to recruit their transmembrane binding partners.
source: These findings elucidate that GPCRs could employ distinct TMs to recruit their transmembrane binding partners.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from comparing different GPCR structures.
